title: The Capabilities, Not the Behaviour
gist: What actually qualifies as an architecture characteristic, the four families they fall into, and why supporting more of them makes the design worse rather than better.
minute: A requirement is an **architecture characteristic** only if it passes all three tests: it is **non-domain**, it **influences structure**, and it is **critical to success**. Fail one and it is a design concern, not an architectural one.
The domain is what the system **does**. Characteristics are what it must be **good at**. Both are structural design; only one of them arrives written down.
**Implicit** characteristics — availability, reliability, security — almost never appear in a requirements document, and you are expected to surface them from domain knowledge anyway.

Four families: **operational** (availability, performance, scalability), **structural** (maintainability, extensibility, portability), **cloud** (on-demand scaling, zone availability, region privacy — new in the 2nd edition) and **cross-cutting** (security, legal, accessibility, privacy).
Each characteristic you support costs design effort and drags the others around with it. **Never strive for the best architecture; aim for the least worst.**

sections.t: Behaviour and capability are different jobs
sections.alt: Two panels — the domain on the left and architecture characteristics on the right — resting on one bar
sections.cap: Fig. 4-1 · both halves are structural design. Only the left half is in the requirements document.
sections.p: Defining characteristics is a large part of what separates architecture from coding and design. Requirements say what the application should do; characteristics say how it is implemented and why those choices were made.
quotes: Never strive for the best architecture; aim for the least worst architecture.
The chapter's own summary, and a working test: if your design maximises everything, you have not chosen anything.

sections.t: Three tests, all of which must pass
sections.alt: A triangle whose three corners are non-domain, structural and critical
sections.cap: Fig. 4-2 · the triangle is deliberate — each corner supports the others, and they pull against each other.
items: **Non-domain design consideration** — it isn't about what the system does. No requirements document says “prevent technical debt”, but it is a real design consideration.
**Influences structure** — it needs special shape, not just careful coding. Ask directly: can I implement this by design, or does it change the architecture?
**Critical or important to success** — every characteristic you support adds complexity, so the aim is the fewest you can get away with, not the most you can name.

sections.t: Is security an architecture characteristic on this project?
sections.alt: Security achievable by design or by structure, above scalability which only structure can achieve
sections.sit: Security matters on every project — every system needs baseline precautions. Does that make it an architecture characteristic *here*, or a coding standard?
opts: It's always architectural. It matters everywhere.
Then so is everything, and the word stops distinguishing anything. Baseline hygiene — encryption, hashing, salting — is design, and a monolith can hold it that way.
It becomes architectural when the architecture must change shape for it.
In a distributed system you build a hardened service with stricter access protocols. That is structure, not hygiene, and it belongs in the characteristics list.
sections.verdict: Security can be met by design *or* by structure, so the answer depends on the system. **Scalability cannot** — no amount of clever design gets a monolith past a certain point; beyond it you change to a distributed style. That's why operational characteristics get the closest attention: they are the ones that most often force structure.

sections.alt: Four columns listing operational, structural, cloud and cross-cutting characteristics
sections.cap: Tables 4-1 to 4-4. Not a standard — a starting vocabulary you are expected to localise.
sections.p: There is no universal list and no authoritative definitions. ISO publishes categories that partly overlap these, and even there the authors disagree with one entry: *functional suitability* describes why you're building the software, not a characteristic of the architecture.
items: Many terms are ambiguous and some overlap. **Interoperability** implies easy integration with other systems, so it implies published, documented APIs; **compatibility** is about industry and domain standards. Different things.
**Availability** and **reliability** look identical until you consider IP, which is available but not reliable — packets arrive out of order and the receiver has to ask again.
**Learnability** has two definitions in current use: how easily users learn the software, and whether the system learns its own environment to self-configure. Pick one and write it down.
The practical answer to all of this is domain-driven design's **ubiquitous language**: your organisation defines its own terms, objectively, and everyone uses those.

sections.alt: A triangle whose three corners are non-domain, structural and critical
sections.sit: You have a full requirements document for a trading system. It specifies the domain in detail. It says nothing about latency, nothing about availability, nothing about recovery. The business considers the document complete.
opts: Build to the document. Anything missing is out of scope.
You will ship a system that does the right things and cannot be relied on to do them. Availability, reliability and security underpin virtually every application and are almost never written down.
Use domain knowledge to surface the implicit characteristics, then confirm them.
A high-frequency trading firm doesn't specify low latency in every document because everyone in that domain already knows. Your job is to know it too, name it, and get it agreed.
sections.verdict: **Explicit** characteristics appear in the requirements. **Implicit** ones are the ones you are expected to find during analysis, using knowledge of the problem domain. The second group is where architects earn their keep — and where a missing one is discovered in production rather than in review.

sections.t: They are synergistic, which is the whole problem
sections.alt: A beam on a fulcrum: raising security lowers performance
sections.cap: Raise one and the others move. Security buys itself with encryption, indirection and hidden secrets — all of which cost time.
sections.p: Pilots learning helicopters find that every control interacts with every other one: changing any input requires adjusting all the rest. Choosing characteristics is that, permanently. This is also why the number of *categories* keeps growing — operations used to be a black box architects ignored, and microservices ended that.

sections.alt: A cost curve rising steeply with the number of characteristics supported
sections.cap: Support for a characteristic is never free: design effort, implementation, maintenance, sometimes structure.
sections.p: Trying to support too many produces a generic solution aimed at every business problem, which becomes unwieldy and rarely works. The mitigation is not to guess better on the first attempt — it is to make the architecture **as iterative as possible**, so that being wrong early costs less. That is the Agile lesson applied one level up.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 4: Architectural Characteristics Defined, pp. 55–65.
